title: Saber and conocer
topic: saber and conocer; the a before a person as direct object
why: After querer, poder and tener que, the lesson separates saber and conocer, the two Spanish verbs for "to know", with a few traps. It also introduces the personal a before a person as direct object, a rule with no English equivalent that you'll use all the time.

{"lessons": ["

Sé and conozco

English has one verb, \"to know\". Spanish has two: one for facts and skills, the other for people and places you're familiar with. Good news on the conjugation side: only the first person is irregular.

saber (to know a fact)conocer (to know a person, a place)
yoséconozco
túsabesconoces
él, ella, ustedsabeconoce
nosotros, nosotrassabemosconocemos
vosotros, vosotrassabéisconocéis
ellos, ellas, ustedessabenconocen

Two forms to watch

  • Sé (I know) has a written accent. Without it, se is the pronoun in se llama or se levanta. The accent makes the difference in writing.
  • Conozco takes a z before the c: conozco. Most verbs ending in -ocer and -ecer do the same, like parecer (to seem).

Everything else is regular -er: sabes, sabe, sabemos; conoces, conoce, conocemos.

No sé (I don't know) is one of the most useful phrases in Spanish. Add a smile and a shrug, and everyone understands.

¿Sabes dónde está Pablo? No sé, no conozco a Pablo.Do you know where Pablo is? I don't know, I don't know Pablo.
", "

Saber or conocer?

VerbUseExample
sabera piece of information, a factSé dónde vive Marta. (I know where Marta lives)
saberknowing the answer to a question¿Sabes a qué hora sale el tren?
saber + infinitiveknowing how to do somethingSé nadar. / ¿Sabes cocinar?
conocera personConozco a Javier.
conocera place, a city, a restaurantConozco Granada. / ¿Conoces este bar?

Traps for an English speaker

  • \"To know the answer, the address, the price\": that's information, so saber: Sé la respuesta.
  • \"To know\" a language: you can say saber inglés but, more often, hablar inglés (to speak English).
  • English \"can\" covers two Spanish verbs. Saber + infinitive is a learned skill (\"know how to\"); poder is what's possible right now. Sé nadar, pero hoy no puedo: hace mucho frío. (I can swim, but I can't today: it's very cold.)

The simplest test: if you can put \"that\", \"where\", \"when\", \"how\" or an infinitive after it, it's saber. Before a person or a place (\"to be familiar with\", \"to have met\"), it's conocer.

No sé bailar flamenco, pero conozco un bar muy bueno en Sevilla.I can't dance flamenco, but I know a very good bar in Seville.
", "

The \"personal a\"

Here's a rule that doesn't exist in English: when the direct object of a verb is a specific person, you put a before it.

A person: aA place or a thing: nothing
Conozco a Marta.Conozco Madrid.
¿Conoces a la profesora?¿Conoces el museo del Prado?
Espero a Diego.Espero el autobús.
Busco a Lucía.Busco las llaves.

And as always, a + el = al: Conozco al profesor de guitarra.

When not to use it

  • Before a thing or a place: Conozco Bilbao, no a.
  • With tener: Tengo dos hermanos, no a.
  • Before an unspecified person: Busco un profesor de español (any teacher at all).

A few Spanish cities

Toledo, Segovia, Granada, Córdoba, Cádiz, Bilbao, San Sebastián, Santiago de Compostela, Salamanca. Watch the accents: Córdoba, Cádiz, San Sebastián, Málaga, León.

¿Conoces Toledo? Sí, y conozco a una chica de Toledo.Do you know Toledo? Yes, and I know a girl from Toledo.
